flashcards.q: What does writing local-first mean?
flashcards.a: The user's change is written to the device's own database first (such as IndexedDB) and goes to the server later, when the network is back.
flashcards.more: The app then responds instantly, even offline. The price is conflicts: if the same thing is changed on two devices, they must be reconciled at sync. That is why the outbox, versions and merge rules matter.

flashcards.q: What is a lost update?
flashcards.a: When two people change the same thing and one change silently wipes out the other without knowing, as in last-write-wins.
flashcards.more: It is the most dangerous kind because nobody notices the mistake. If the conflict isn't detected, there is no chance to reconcile. So the first step of the solution is detecting the conflict.

flashcards.q: How does a base version catch a conflict?
flashcards.a: The client sends the version it wrote against with its change. If the server's version differs, the server doesn't write and returns 409.
flashcards.more: In Doctrine, a `#[ORM\Version]` field and `LockMode::OPTIMISTIC` do this together. If they match, the write happens and the version goes up; if not, an `OptimisticLockException` is thrown.

flashcards.q: Why is a timestamp a poor way to catch conflicts?
flashcards.a: The phone's and the server's clocks disagree. A wrong clock can make an old change look new and delete correct data. A version number is reliable.
flashcards.more: A user can change the phone's clock themselves, and NTP jumps can set time backwards. So decide order using a server-side counter that only grows, not the device's time.

flashcards.q: When is last-write-wins acceptable, and when is it not?
flashcards.a: It is fine for low-importance fields. For money, stock or important text it is not, because one person's work silently disappears.
flashcards.more: LWW is popular because it is simple, but it isn't a decision, it's a rule for throwing data away. In most apps, combining field-level merge with asking the user is the safe way to go.

flashcards.q: What are version vectors and CRDTs used for?
flashcards.a: A version vector tells you whether two changes were concurrent. A CRDT is a structure that merges to the same result in any order.
flashcards.more: A version vector keeps a separate counter per device. A simple CRDT example is sending changes like "+2 cartons", which give the same total whatever the order. An ordinary app rarely needs them.

flashcards.q: What should each change in an offline outbox contain?
flashcards.a: Its own id (a UUID), what is being changed, the base version, and the change data. The id lets the server spot duplicates.
flashcards.more: When the connection drops and the reply is lost, the client sends the same change again. The server recognizes the id and says "already applied", so the change isn't applied twice. The outbox lives in IndexedDB, not in memory.

flashcards.q: Why can one user's second offline edit conflict with their own first edit?
flashcards.a: Both edits were written against the same base version. Once the first is accepted the server moves on, so the second looks stale and gets a 409.
flashcards.more: The fix is to rebase: when the server accepts an edit it returns the new version, and the phone copies it into every later edit of that note. If the first edit is refused, the later ones are parked with it, because they were built on top of it.

flashcards.q: Why is polling expensive at scale?
flashcards.a: Every user sends a request at a fixed interval, and most come back "nothing changed". The server pays full price even when nothing has changed.
flashcards.more: If 10,000 users poll every 2 seconds, that is 5,000 requests per second. The status may change only about three times an hour, so push needs just a few messages per second.

flashcards.q: What is SSE (Server-Sent Events)?
flashcards.a: One-way messages from server to browser over a single open HTTP connection. The browser listens with `EventSource`.
flashcards.more: Because it is plain HTTP, there is less trouble with proxies, auth and load balancers. If the connection drops, the browser reconnects by itself. To send from browser to server, you still need a separate POST.

flashcards.q: How do you choose between SSE and WebSocket?
flashcards.a: If the server only sends news, use SSE. If both sides talk a lot, as in chat, games or collaborative editors, use WebSocket.
flashcards.more: WebSocket is a separate protocol, so you handle reconnect, auth and scaling yourself. Most business apps need "tell me when the status changes", which SSE does easily.

flashcards.q: What is long-polling?
flashcards.a: The client sends a request and the server holds the reply until something new arrives. After getting it, the client sends another request.
flashcards.more: Fewer empty requests go out than with plain polling. But every change needs a new connection, and you write the reconnect code yourself. Before SSE arrived, this was the usual route.

flashcards.q: What is Mercure, and what is Symfony's role?
flashcards.a: Mercure is a hub that holds the SSE connections. Symfony just calls `HubInterface::publish(new Update(...))` to hand it a message.
flashcards.more: Holding the connections is the hub's job, so PHP-FPM doesn't have to carry many open connections. For personal data, `private: true` makes the hub check that the subscriber's JWT grants access to the topic.

flashcards.q: What are the three precautions when using EventSource in Vue?
flashcards.a: Re-fetch the current state each time the stream opens, pass `withCredentials: true` for private topics, and call `close()` on unmount.
flashcards.more: Changes made before the stream opens, or while it was down, never arrive on it, so a plain GET on every open brings the true state. Without `close()`, every visit to the page leaves one more connection behind.

flashcards.q: How do you measure presence (who is online) reliably?
flashcards.a: The client sends a regular heartbeat and the server keeps a Redis key with a TTL. When the TTL runs out the key vanishes, and the user counts as offline.
flashcards.more: Looking only at "is the connection open" gives wrong answers, because mobile connections die silently and the server doesn't notice. Keep the heartbeat interval at about half the TTL, so losing one beat is survivable.

flashcards.q: How do you reach a user who has the app closed?
flashcards.a: With a push notification (FCM or Web Push). It needs no open connection; the message travels through the phone's OS.
flashcards.more: Keep push messages short, and when the user opens the app, fetch the current state from the server. The message only rings the bell; it isn't the source of truth.

flashcards.q: What is fan-out?
flashcards.a: Spreading something one person creates (like a post) to many people, for example into every follower's feed.
flashcards.more: The question is when to do the spreading: when the post is written (write-time), or when the feed is opened (read-time). The follower counts and the read-to-write ratio decide.

flashcards.q: What is write-time fan-out, and what does it cost?
flashcards.a: When a post is written, put it into every follower's feed. Feed reads are fast, but the write work scales with the number of followers.
flashcards.more: A separate copy per follower also takes more space. But feeds are read far more often than written, so this way usually pays off.

flashcards.q: When is read-time fan-out the right one?
flashcards.a: When reads are rare and writes frequent, or follower counts are huge. The post is written once and joined with everyone else's when the feed is read.
flashcards.more: Feed reads are slow because they must join and sort every time. Whoever follows the most people gets the slowest feed. So on its own this way is rarely used for ordinary feeds.

flashcards.q: What is the celebrity (hot key) problem?
flashcards.a: One post from a user with a huge following creates millions of writes under write-time, filling the queue and delaying everyone else's posts.
flashcards.more: One user jamming the whole system is the hot key. The fix is hybrid: don't fan out celebrities' posts; fetch and merge them separately when a feed is read.

flashcards.q: How does hybrid fan-out work?
flashcards.a: Posts from users below the follower threshold are fanned out at write time. Celebrities' posts are fetched at feed-read time and merged into the user's own feed.
flashcards.more: Reads stay cheap for ordinary followees, and a celebrity's post doesn't create millions of writes. Fetching the posts of the few celebrities a user follows when the feed opens is cheap work.

flashcards.q: Why is a Redis sorted set good for a feed?
flashcards.a: With the time as the score you can read newest-to-oldest quickly, and adding the same member again creates no duplicate.
flashcards.more: `ZADD` is idempotent, so redelivery of a message leaves the feed correct. `ZREMRANGEBYRANK` keeps each feed small, at about 800 items. The real data lives in the posts table; Redis is only a cache.

flashcards.q: In a feed, offset or cursor for paging, and what goes in the cursor?
flashcards.a: A cursor, because it stays stable when new posts arrive. It holds the (time, id) pair of the last post shown: "older, or the same time with a smaller id".
flashcards.more: Posts can share a millisecond. Sort and cut by time alone and two posts with equal times come out in random order, so one can be skipped or shown twice at a page boundary. Adding the id pins the order.

flashcards.q: Why does a feed cursor of just the time drop posts?
flashcards.a: Posts that share the last post's millisecond but did not fit on the page are "not older", so the next page skips them for good.
flashcards.more: Example: posts 9, 8 and 7 all at the same millisecond, page size 2. Page 1 is 9 and 8; "older than that time" excludes 7 forever. Reading the same-time posts with a smaller id as well fixes it.

flashcards.q: Why send a fan-out in chunks of 1,000 followers instead of one big message?
flashcards.a: If a long job crashes midway, a retry redoes all of it. Chunks with a checkpoint redo at most one chunk of 1,000.
flashcards.more: Each message carries the last follower id it reached, so the next chunk starts from there. With 10,000 followers, a crash at 6,000 redoes 10,000 as one job, but at most 1,000 in chunks.
